steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR): drafted in 1950, ratified by the UK in 1951. Protects fundamental rights: right to life (Article 2), prohibition of torture (Article 3), right to liberty (Article 5), right to a fair trial (Article 6), right to privacy (Article 8), freedom of expression (Article 10), freedom of assembly (Article 11), and right to marry (Article 12).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Human Rights Act 1998: incorporated ECHR rights into UK law. UK courts can now hear human rights cases without going to Strasbourg. Courts can declare legislation 'incompatible' with the ECHR (but cannot strike it down - Parliament decides). Public authorities (including the government, police, councils) must act compatibly with ECHR rights.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Key rights explained: Right to life (Article 2): the state must not take life arbitrarily and must investigate deaths. Right to a fair trial (Article 6): independent tribunal, presumption of innocence, right to legal representation. Freedom of expression (Article 10): can say what you think BUT restrictions apply (hate speech, defamation, national security).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Balancing rights: rights are not absolute - they can be limited where necessary and proportionate. Freedom of expression vs protection from hate speech. Right to privacy vs freedom of the press (Max Mosley case). Right to liberty vs national security (terrorism legislation). Courts balance rights on a case-by-case basis.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Describe the key rights protected by the ECHR and explain how the Human Rights Act 1998 protects them in UK law. | Q: Explain how courts balance competing human rights, using examples. | Q: Evaluate whether the UK should remain bound by the ECHR.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: ECHR = 14+ rights (life, liberty, fair trial, privacy, expression, assembly). HRA 1998 = makes them enforceable in UK courts. Rights can CONFLICT. Courts balance using PROPORTIONALITY: restrictions must be necessary, proportionate and for a legitimate aim. Leave ECHR = more sovereignty but WEAKER rights protection. Stay = stronger protection but less sovereignty.
